turns.t: Mrs Pettigrew, I've got the letter from your GP here, saying you've an acid taste in your mouth. How are you getting on? ~
Well. Yes. It's. Um. ~
Take your time. Tell me in your own words. ~
In the mornings. There's this taste. Sour. In my mouth. When I wake up, every morning.
A sour taste in the mouth first thing, every morning. Is that right?
Yes. It's like, um, vinegar. ~
How long has it been going on? ~
A few weeks. Maybe. I don't. It's hard to say. ~
That's fine. Does anything bring it on, like a late meal? ~
I suppose. I do like my supper. Late. With the telly. ~
And does it ever happen at other times of day, or only on waking? ~
Only when I wake. Not later. ~
Any actual chest pain, like a heaviness or a squeezing?
No. Nothing like that. No chest pain.
That's helpful, thank you. Any allergies to medicines or food?
No allergies. None.
Good. Do you have any health problems I should know about?
Asthma. Just a little, since I was young.
Thank you. Let me feel your tummy, if that's all right. Could you lie back on the couch? ~
Oh. Yes. Of course. ~
Tell me if anything is tender.
Mm. No. It's fine. ~
Your abdomen is soft and not tender anywhere.
Good. ~
Let me repeat what you've told me. A sour taste every morning for a few weeks, and a late supper in front of the telly. ~
Yes. That's it. ~
There are simple things you can do. Try to finish supper at least three hours before bed.
Three hours. Oh. That's early. ~
And raise the head of the bed a little, with a couple of extra pillows, or a wedge.
A wedge? ~
A foam wedge. You can get one from a pharmacy. ~
I could try. ~
Also, cut back on tea and coffee in the evening, and see how you go. ~
I'll try. ~
Good. Do that for a few weeks. If it's not settled in four weeks, come back and see me.
Four weeks. Yes. I'll write it down. ~
Lovely. Any questions before you go? ~
No. No, thank you, doctor. ~
